newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss wartime probe under pressure for fast facts.
newsitem.headline: Swiss wartime probe under pressure for fast facts.

text.p: The historian leading Switzerland's sweeping review of its World War Two financial role says his international commission will unveil its first findings by mid-year amid political pressure to produce fast results.

Jean-Francois Bergier said the government, which appointed his commission in December under fire from world Jewish groups, wanted facts quickly in order to decide how much to pay into a Holocaust memorial fund agreed last week with Swiss banks.
"Our role is to underpin this decision," Bergier, an economic history specialist at Zurich's Federal Institute of Technology (ETH), told Reuters in a weekend interview.

Only afterwards will the commission face the full breadth of its mandate, set by federal decree as an "historical and legal investigation of the fate of assets which reached Switzerland as a result of National Socialist (Nazi) rule".
"This is a huge task...We don't yet know what documents we will need and how far back they will reach," Bergier said.

The commission of eight historians and one legal expert includes four Swiss, an Israeli historian, a former Polish foreign minister, a Princeton University professor and a senior historian at the Holocaust Museum in Washington D.C.

Bergier said he understood the Federal Council, or cabinet, was pushing for facts on gold purchases and refugee policy so it could announce a memorial fund payment that may calm critics led by the World Jewish Congress.
"I agreed under political pressure. But in fact it does not please me and it would be better to proceed methodically," Bergier said.

Still busy organising the commission's work and staff, Bergier said it was too early to forecast exactly when the reports on Swiss National Bank (SNB) purchases of Nazi gold and Berne's wartime refugee policy would be ready.
"I told the cabinet that we should be able to finish the reports by summer," he said. "It is fairly easy with the Swiss National Bank because the facts are known."
The SNB says it made around 20 million Swiss francs ($14 million) in profit buying a net 1.2 billion francs worth of gold, much of it looted from occupied countries, from Hitler's central bank.
Berne's wartime policy of rejecting many Jewish asylum seekers and charging Jewish groups 55 million Swiss francs to care for those who were admitted has also been well documented.

The commission, armed with unprecedented power to lift bank secrecy and demand historical records, is still assembling a research staff that may total around 20 people on an initial budget of five million Swiss francs for five years.

It meets for the first time in early May to draft a strategy for tackling subjects as diverse as the scope of Jewish wealth hidden in neutral Switzerland, Nazi accounts at Swiss banks and Swiss purchases of companies Hitler wrested from Jewish owners.
"The research will take at least three years...But perhaps we can settle much of the difficult issues with our interim reports," Bergier said. The panel plans to brief the cabinet every six months.

Any information that could identify Jewish accounts unclaimed since their owners were killed in the Holocaust will immediately be turned over to another commission set up by Swiss banks and Jewish groups to trace such missing wealth.

Bergier said the sheer mass of records at Swiss banks, insurance companies, lawyers' offices and other sources meant researchers would have to rely in part on the help of the banks and other companies themselves.

But he said the banks especially were under tremendous pressure to cooperate due to negative publicity over Holocaust accounts and the recent shredding of old records at Union Bank of Switzerland, which UBS called an accident.

"The banks have to do something, otherwise they will lose their credibility," he said. "Usually we historians can tell whether data are complete or not...If not, then we will have to check on them ourselves." ($1=1.4260 Swiss Franc)
